title: Chlamydia trachomatis
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: A common sexually transmitted bacterium that infects the urogenital tract, causing urethritis, PID and neonatal conjunctivitis. Diagnosis relies on NAAT; treatment is doxycycline or azithromycin. Early detection prevents long‑term sequelae.

sections.p: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular, cell‑wall‑free bacterium that spreads through sexual contact. In East Africa it is the leading cause of urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in young adults.
It has a biphasic life cycle: elementary bodies (infectious) and reticulate bodies (replicative). It evades immunity by intracellular residence and antigenic variation.
b: No cell wall – no beta‑lactam activity

sections.p: Spread by unprotected vaginal, anal or oral sex. In the host, elementary bodies enter epithelial cells, convert to reticulate bodies, replicate, then reform elementary bodies that exit to infect new cells.
b: Can persist for months if untreated

sections.p: In men: urethritis with dysuria, mucopurulent discharge. In women: cervicitis, PID, ectopic pregnancy risk. Neonates: conjunctivitis, pneumonia.
b: PID severity graded by CDC: mild, moderate, severe

sections.p: NAAT on urine or endocervical swab is gold standard. In low‑resource settings, rapid antigen tests are available but less sensitive.

t.b: Detects Chlamydia DNA – positive means active infection
Quick screening – negative may miss infection; confirm with NAAT if available
Treats all stages; avoids resistance seen with azithromycin
Convenient single dose; useful where adherence is poor

sections.p: Remember: asymptomatic in 70% of women; PID can present with lower abdominal pain and cervical motion tenderness. In resource‑poor settings, treat empirically if high suspicion and NAAT unavailable.
b: Look for cervical motion tenderness (Chandelier sign)

sections.p: Gonorrhoea (both cause urethritis) but gonorrhoea responds to ceftriaxone; Chlamydia is resistant to beta‑lactams.
False negatives in early infection; antigen tests less sensitive; culture requires specialised media not available locally.
If severe PID (fever >38.5°C, rebound tenderness, vomiting) admit for IV antibiotics and monitor for sepsis.
Repeat NAAT 3 months after treatment to confirm cure; counsel on safe sex practices.
Screen all pregnant women and high‑risk groups; treat neonates with erythromycin eye drops to prevent blindness.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with fever, vomiting, or signs of sepsis; infertility concerns; neonatal eye discharge

faq.q: Why is Chlamydia often asymptomatic in women?
faq.a: Its intracellular life cycle evades immune detection, leading to mild or no symptoms.
Yes, untreated PID damages fallopian tubes, increasing ectopic pregnancy risk.

faq.q: Is a single dose of azithromycin effective?
faq.a: It is effective for most infections but resistance is rising; doxycycline is preferred where adherence is reliable.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with lower abdominal pain and cervical motion tenderness. What is the next best step? — Perform a cervical swab for NAAT; start empiric doxycycline and ceftriaxone if PID is suspected.
A neonate has red, watery eyes at birth. What prophylaxis should be given? — Apply erythromycin ophthalmic ointment immediately.
A patient on doxycycline develops a rash. What is the likely cause? — Drug‑induced hypersensitivity; discontinue doxycycline and switch to azithromycin.
A 30‑year‑old man has urethral discharge but negative Gram stain. What is the most likely organism? — Chlamydia trachomatis; confirm with NAAT.
